turns.q: Is Amazon's earnings quality deteriorating? Put operating cash flow beside net income for the last eight quarters, show the accruals ratio trend, tell me whether receivables and inventory are growing faster than revenue over the same windows, and say what that means for the size of our AMZN position.
turns.answer:
Amazon’s earnings quality does not look like it is deteriorating on this window; if anything, the cash picture is still mixed rather than clearly worsening.
On operating cash flow versus net income for the last eight quarters, operating cash flow stayed well above net income in every quarter shown. The series starts at $25.28B versus $13.48B on 2024-06-30 and ends at $26.03B versus $30.25B on 2026-03-31. The pattern is volatile — for example, operating cash flow spikes to $45.64B on 2024-12-31 and $54.46B on 2025-12-31, then falls back to $17.02B on 2025-03-31 and $26.03B on 2026-03-31 — but it is not a clean cash deterioration versus earnings.
The accruals ratio trend is also not showing a steady deterioration. It runs from -2.13% on 2024-06-30 to -1.82% on 2024-09-30, -4.10% on 2024-12-31, 0.02% on 2025-03-31, -2.10% on 2025-06-30, -1.97% on 2025-09-30, -4.07% on 2025-12-31, and 0.46% on 2026-03-31. That is choppy, but mostly negative, which argues against earnings being propped up by accruals over most of the period. The latest reading is slightly positive at 0.46%, so the newest quarter is less favorable than the earlier negative readings, but not enough by itself to call the trend deteriorating.
Receivables are the clearer weak spot. Accounts receivable rises from $50.11B on 2024-06-30 to $75.53B on 2026-03-31, while revenue rises from $148B to $182B. That means receivables are growing faster than revenue over the period shown, which is a negative earnings-quality signal because more sales are sitting unpaid.
Inventory is less concerning on the same comparison. It moves from $34.11B on 2024-06-30 to $36.53B on 2026-03-31, while revenue rises from $148B to $182B. Inventory is not growing faster than revenue over the full window, so it is not adding the same pressure.
For the AMZN position, the current weight is 7.03% and issuer concentration for AMZN is also 7.03%. That is a meaningful but not large position in this book. Given the evidence, I would not use earnings quality alone to argue for a forced reduction; the bigger caution is the receivables build, which says to watch working-capital drag and collection quality. If you want a tighter stance, the main reason would be that receivables are outrunning revenue, not that cash conversion has clearly broken.
If you want, I can next compare this against AMZN’s prior four-quarter pattern or put the same checks beside another held name for context.

{"text": "Probably yes for net margins, but I would not call it broad-based “margin expansion” across the whole P&L with high confidence.

The desk could not compute gross margin or operating margin for LLY because those methods are not held here: gross_margin was not computed because LLY reports no gross_profit with a period, and operating_margin was not computed because LLY reports no operating_income with a period. It also does not hold revenue as a filed fact, and it does not hold selling_general_and_administrative or research_and_development as names. So the clean read is on the lines it does hold and on management’s own explanation.

On net margin, the recent pattern is strong. LLY’s net margin moved from 26.2% [f_fea280146d67] on 2024-06-30 to 37.4% [f_fea280146d67] on 2026-03-31, with the path showing 8.48%, 32.6%, 21.7%, 36.4%, 31.7%, 34.4%, and 37.4% across the eight quarters [f_fea280146d67]. That is already expansion, not just stability.

The filing points to the main support as higher gross margin. Management says, “Net income and earnings per share increased in 2025, primarily due to higher gross margin, partially offset by increased marketing, selling, and administrative expenses and research and development expenses.” It also says, “Revenue increased in 2025 driven primarily by increased volume, partially offset by lower realized prices. The increased volume and lower realized prices in 2025 were primarily driven by Mounjaro and Zepbound.” That is a mixed message for next year: volume and mix are helping, but lower realized prices are a real offset.

What I would take from the cost lines is that pressure is still there, even if net margin has held up. Cost of revenue rose from $2.17B [f_3ddb67183448] on 2024-06-30 to $3.58B [f_3ddb67183448] on 2026-03-31, while income tax expense rose from $550M [f_3bdaa2a4914f] to $1.45B [f_3bdaa2a4914f] over the same span. Nonoperating interest expense is also not disappearing: it was $180M [f_762feedc8fd4] on 2024-03-31 and $223M [f_762feedc8fd4] on 2025-12-31, with a peak of $249M [f_762feedc8fd4] on 2025-06-30. Those items do not negate margin expansion, but they mean the expansion is being earned, not automatic.

The key reason I would still lean “yes” is the product mix and pipeline in Item 7. The filing shows Mounjaro and Zepbound driving volume, and it also lists multiple approved or advanced programs across cardiometabolic health, immunology, neuroscience, and oncology. That supports continued mix improvement if launch execution stays strong. But the filing itself also flags that lower realized prices are already offsetting some of the volume benefit, and it explicitly warns that risks and uncertainties in Item 1A could cause actual results to differ.

So my read for this book is: LLY’s margin trend is still favorable, and the latest net margin print argues the market is not seeing deterioration. But next year’s expansion is likely to be more incremental than linear, because price pressure, higher cost of revenue, and continuing tax and interest drag could cap how much further the net margin can widen. If I were changing my view, I would want to see whether the next filing says higher volume is again outpacing lower realized prices, or whether pricing and cost inflation start to dominate."}
